$comment: The write-path registry (issue #200). Every place in the workspace that can land a spec op is declared here, and scripts/check-write-paths.mjs refuses a call site that is not — an allowlist, so a new way to write the spec is a failure until somebody declares and covers it, rather than a silent pass. Read alongside packages/spec/src/base/actor.ts (the `surface` vocabulary and why attribution is a record rather than a gate) and docs/write-paths.md (the policy).

$fields.id: Stable identifier, also stamped as `actor.path` on every op this path lands, so a log entry points back at its declaration.
$fields.surface: One of OP_SURFACES in packages/spec/src/base/actor.ts. The checker refuses an unknown value.
$fields.site: Workspace-relative file where the path *is* — the command, loader or installer a reviewer would go read.
$fields.via: Optional: the shared file that calls applyOp on this path's behalf, when that is not `site` itself (five CLI verbs share lib/land.ts; the workbench form applies through view-model.ts). Every applyOp call site in the workspace must be named as some path's `site` or `via`.
$fields.kind: `write` persists to the spec store. `preflight` applies to a local clone it discards — a validate or a preview, never a write. The invariant suite asserts the difference rather than trusting the label.
$fields.authorKind: Which `origin` values this path can stamp: `ai`, `human`, or `either`.
$fields.grounds: Whether rows this path lands are immediately grounding (accepted). Only meaningful for `write`.
$fields.canAccept: Whether this path may flip an existing row's isAccepted null->true — i.e. whether it may settle a review. The most consequential declaration in this file.
$fields.acceptRationale: Required whenever canAccept is true: why this path is entitled to settle a decision on a human's behalf. Checked for presence rather than the count of such paths being capped, because a cap is satisfiable by a two-character diff and a written justification is not. Printed by the checker on every successful run, so the set stays visible.
$fields.coveredBy: The invariant test that names this id. The checker fails when the file does not exist or does not mention the id.
$fields.why: Why this path exists and what a reviewer should understand about it.

paths.why: The agent's authorized write — `apply_spec_change`, and `record_decision` through the same helper. Rows land accepted with AI provenance so the running app can see them (issue #70); what makes that safe is that the op is logged, diffed, attributed and revertible, not that it was blocked.

`validateOpDryRun` — the one validator `propose_spec_change` and `apply_spec_change` share (issue #71). Applies to a clone to find the errors a save would raise, then throws the clone away. This is the suggest half of suggest->accept, and it must never write.
`maxstack op` — the raw typed op, the honest primitive under the sugar verbs.
`maxstack add-entity` — sugar compiling to data.addEntity (issue #20).
`maxstack add-field` — sugar compiling to data.addField.
`maxstack add-page` — sugar compiling to page.addPage (issue #95).

`maxstack theme` — a theme.set op (issue #127). The theme is not a provenanced row, so there is nothing here to review; it is declared because it still lands an op-log entry and that entry needs attribution.

`maxstack start` lands the blueprint the AI drafted from a sentence (issue #191). Always `origin: 'ai'` whoever typed the command, because the spec is machine-authored either way — the whole point of the entry path is that the user did not write it.

paths.acceptRationale: The terminal half of the same review (issue #199), entitled to it on exactly the same terms as the pane: it calls the same planBulkReview and inherits the same refusals, and it deliberately has no --all and no --force, so there is no way to talk it into clearing a high-risk proposal that the workbench would not.
paths.why: `maxstack review` — the queue with risk classification, bulk accept/reject, and --undo. Exists because an unattended agent session is what produces forty pending proposals, and a queue only a browser can clear is a queue that stays full.

paths.acceptRationale: The author accepting their own change with --accept, in a trusted-solo invocation. Entitled to it because it claims nothing else: the review op carries the SAME actor as the op it settles, so the trail says “the author cleared this” rather than implying a second party reviewed it.
paths.why: The shared apply -> (accept) -> (gen) pipeline behind every CLI write verb, and the fallback attribution for a caller that supplies none. `canAccept` because `--accept` emits a cascading provenance.review — stamped with the *same* actor as the op it settles, so the trail says the author accepted their own change rather than implying somebody reviewed it.

`applyBundle` lowers a bundle's runtime into ops on install. Rows land `manual()` and `origin: 'human'` because installing a module is a human act whoever typed it; the `bundle` surface plus the slug is what makes it reviewable as one unit instead of N unexplained hand-authored entities.
`validateBundleApply` advances a local system op by op to collect every structural collision rather than only the first. The system is local and discarded with the error list.

A bundle upgrade's codemods, idempotent by construction (issue #195). `origin: 'human'` because only `maxstack upgrade` runs them and a person invokes that; the `codemod` surface is what tells a reviewer an upgrade rewrote a declaration they never touched.

paths.acceptRationale: The workbench accept/reject form — a person clicking a button about one named row. This is the path every other one is measured against; if it were not entitled to settle a review, nothing would be.
paths.why: The workbench accept/reject form — the human review surface, and the only write path whose entire purpose is to settle somebody else's suggestion. Reaches `applyOp` through `applyReviewAction` in view-model.ts.

The workbench asking “what are you trying to build?” and writing the answer down (issue #256). Lands the maintainer's own sentence as a product-layer requirement via `prd.addRequirement`, `origin: 'human'` because they typed it — their goal must not end up attributed to whichever agent later writes the code for it. Reuses the existing product vocabulary rather than inventing an `intent` concept, so `query_spec {section:"product"}` returns it and the agent reads the intent out of the spec instead of being told it in a prompt that vanishes with the conversation. `canAccept: false` and asserted so: writing down a goal must never settle somebody else's pending proposal, and this is the only write path on this surface that a user reaches without first being shown a row to decide about.

The workbench's Land button — an accepted Issue's candidate op, landed by a maintainer who read the Issue and clicked. It reaches applyOp through `apply_spec_change` in packages/mcp/src/tools.ts, reused as an in-process library rather than served over MCP, which is why it needs its own declaration: before issue #358 it borrowed `mcp-apply-spec-change`'s id and surface wholesale, so a browser form post recorded `{origin: 'ai', surface: 'mcp'}` — an agent write that never happened — and the checker passed it because the call *site* was already accounted for. `origin: 'human'` because a person decided to land it; the AI lineage of the op's content lives in the decision-ledger entry landed alongside it. `canAccept: false`: landing writes a new row, it never settles somebody else's pending one.

paths.acceptRationale: A person clearing many rows at once, entitled to it only because it cannot clear a dangerous one: risk defaults to high and every rule only lowers it, so access-control fields, portal-exposed entities, flags and unrecognised kinds are refused a place in the batch rather than swept along with it.
paths.why: Bulk accept/reject and its undo (issue #199) — the third path allowed to settle a review, and the most dangerous button in the product, because it is the one that makes not-looking efficient. What earns it that permission is that it CANNOT clear a high-risk proposal: risk classification defaults to high and every rule only lowers it, so an access-control field, a portal-exposed entity, a flag or an unrecognised kind is refused a place in a batch rather than swept along with twenty field additions. Lands atomically (the model folds onto a private chain; the host persists once) and stamps the batch id in actor.session, so the trail is N per-artifact entries reading as one unit of work rather than one entry claiming somebody reviewed "a batch".
`computeHypotheticalSpec` — the 'if accepted' render behind the structural diff pane. A read dressed as an apply: the result is rendered and dropped, never handed to `spec.save`.

The demo spec the workbench boots against with no project on disk, seeded so every provenance state is visible in the tree. Stamped `harness` rather than `web`: seeded rows must not read as somebody's real work.

`init {ops, apply:true}` — the agent's batch write. Same guarantee as `mcp-apply-spec-change` (logged, diffed, attributed, revertible, one op-log entry per op — a batch is a way of *sending* ops, never a way of landing one entry that claims to be several), with one property that only a batch needs: it is all-or-nothing. Every op is validated against the projection the previous ops produce, and the store is written exactly once, at the end, from a chain that already validated whole. A half-applied batch would leave the spec in a state nobody designed and nobody consented to, which is strictly worse than the fifty single calls it replaces. `apply` defaults to false precisely because this path grounds: forty rows landing accepted is the volume review exists to slow down, so committing is something the caller says out loud.

The in-memory fold `init` runs over a batch before it commits anything — what makes op 2 able to name the entity op 1 adds, and what produces the single merged blast radius a caller consents to. Applied to a local system and only ever read; the ids it spends are the fixed string `op-init-projection-N`, never `ctx.nextOpId()`, so a previewed batch cannot advance the real op counter and a leaked projection is findable by name. Same shape and same danger as `attention-hypothetical`: if this reached `spec.save`, a *proposal* would silently become a write while looking exactly like the feature working.

`specIfAllAccepted` — the 'if you accept everything pending' projection behind the blast radius and the public-exposure category of the what-needs-you report (issue #198). Every pending accept is applied to a local system and the result is only ever read: it is what lets a reviewer see the consequences before consenting to them. The single most dangerous thing on this surface would be for that projection to reach `spec.save`, because opening the workbench would then settle every review in the queue while looking exactly like the feature working — so the ops are stamped `actor.path: 'attention-hypothetical'` to be findable by name if one ever leaks, and both hosts assert the spec and the op log are untouched after a load.

The fixture project the SEO gate (#432) builds, serves and crawls — a site, a public collection portal whose bound admits some rows and not others, a token portal and a paused one. It is a `write` rather than a `preflight` because it genuinely encodes a spec directory to disk; what makes it safe is *where*, not whether: the directory is an `mkdtemp` under the OS temp dir, handed to the server as MAXSTACK_DATA_DIR and removed in a `finally`. It never resolves a project path and never calls `spec.save`, so it cannot reach a real store even when the gate fails partway. Stamped `harness` on `web-demo-seed`'s reasoning: a spec the gate invented must not read as somebody's real work.
